words.note: You know you shouldn't, but you fail to hold back. 「つい食べすぎた」= I ended up eating too much. Carries a tone of self-reproach.
A mistake made because your attention slipped. 「うっかり忘れた」= I forgot by accident. The focus is on carelessness.
An unconscious, instinctive reaction. 「思わず笑った」= I laughed involuntarily. No self-reproach.

c:cf-73.tip: 「つい」= couldn't resist (self-reproach), 「うっかり」= lapse of attention (carelessness), 「思わず」= instinctive reaction (neutral).
eg: I'm on a diet, but I ended up eating the cake. (failed self-control)
I forgot the appointment by mistake. (carelessness)
It was so funny that I laughed without meaning to. (instinct)

words.note: Must be used with a negative. Extremely low frequency. 「めったに会えない」= I can hardly ever see them.
Must be used with a negative. Means insufficient or half-hearted. 「ろくに食べていない」= I haven't been eating properly. Implies dissatisfaction.
Used with affirmative forms. Low frequency, but it does happen. 「たまに映画を見る」= I occasionally watch movies. Neutral.

c:cf-74.tip: 「めったに」= hardly ever (+ negative), 「ろくに」= not properly (+ negative, dissatisfaction), 「たまに」= once in a while (+ affirmative).
eg: I can hardly ever see him. (hardly ever)
I haven't slept properly. (insufficient)
Let's eat out once in a while. (occasionally)

words.note: Stresses that even to the highest degree, it has no effect. 「いくら説明しても分からない」= No matter how much I explain, they don't understand.
Stresses that conditions make no difference. 「どんなに辛くても頑張る」= No matter how hard it is, I'll do my best.
A concessive hypothetical. 「たとえ反対されても、やる」= Even if I'm opposed, I'll do it.

c:cf-75.tip: 「いくら」 stresses degree (however much), 「どんなに」 stresses conditions (whatever the extent), 「たとえ」 stresses a hypothetical concession (even if).
eg: No matter how much I asked, they wouldn't lend it to me.
No matter how busy I am, I eat breakfast.
Even if I fail, I won't regret it.

words.note: A positive cause. Expresses gratitude to a person or thing for a good result. 「先生のおかげで合格した」.
A negative cause. Blames a person or thing. 「雨のせいで中止になった」. Carries a tone of blame.
A neutral cause. Can be used for good or bad outcomes. 「台風のために電車が止まった」. An objective statement.

c:cf-76.tip: Good result, gratitude → 「おかげで」; bad result, blame → 「せいで」; neutral, objective → 「ために」. The tone match is often tested on exams.
eg: Thanks to everyone, it was a success. (gratitude)
It's his fault I was late. (blame)
The road is congested because of an accident. (objective)

words.note: Partial concession followed by a contrast. 「読んだことは読んだが、理解できなかった」= I did read it, but I didn't understand it.
Nearly synonymous with the former. 「高いには高いが、品質はいい」= It is expensive, but the quality is good.

c:cf-77.tip: Both express a partial concession ("I did it, but…" / "it is so, but…") followed by a contrast. 「ことは」 is more natural with verbs, 「には」 with adjectives.
eg: I did eat it, but it wasn't tasty.
It is convenient, but the price is high.

words.note: Corrects a description with a more accurate one. 「頭がいいというより、努力家だ」= He's not so much smart as hardworking.
Substitution or compensation. 「行けないかわりに、プレゼントを送る」= Since I can't go, I'll send a gift in return.
Strong denial. 「上手どころか、ひどいものだ」= Far from being good, it's terrible.

c:cf-78.tip: 「というより」 corrects a description (not A, but rather B), 「かわりに」 means substitution or compensation, 「どころか」 is a strong denial that reverses expectations.
eg: It's not so much cold as I'm nearly freezing.
I read a book instead of watching TV.
Far from decreasing, it's increasing.

words.note: Formal/written. The timing is uncertain but it will surely happen. 「いずれ分かる」= You'll understand sooner or later. Also means "which one."

words.m: before long; one of these days
words.note: Colloquial. 「そのうち行くよ」= I'll go one of these days. Casual tone; it may never happen.
An unspecified day in the future. Carries hope or dreams. 「いつか行きたい」= I want to go someday.

c:cf-79.tip: 「いずれ」 is formal and will surely happen, 「そのうち」 is casual and not necessarily, 「いつか」 carries dreams or hope.
eg: Sooner or later, the truth will come out. (formal, inevitable)
I'll come visit you one of these days. (casual)
Someday I want to travel around the world. (dream)

words.note: ① With a negative: 「さっぱり分からない」= I don't understand at all. ② Describes a clean, light feel: 「さっぱりした味」= a light, refreshing taste.
Feeling good in mind or body. 「すっきりした」= I feel refreshed. Emphasizes the change from discomfort to comfort.
From blurry to clear. 「はっきり言う」= to say it clearly. 「はっきり見える」= to see clearly.
Not a hair off. 「きっちり10時に来た」= He arrived at exactly 10 o'clock. 「きっちり計算する」= to calculate precisely.

c:cf-80.tip: 「さっぱり」 = not at all / refreshing, 「すっきり」 = refreshed, 「はっきり」 = clear and distinct, 「きっちり」 = exact. These mimetic words often appear in N2 listening and reading.
eg: I don't understand this problem at all.
I took a shower and felt refreshed.
Please state your opinion clearly.
Keep strictly to the deadline.

words.note: Movement from far to near, or change from the past up to now. 「暖かくなってきた」= it has gotten warmer. 「持ってくる」= bring.

words.m: ~ is going away from the speaker
words.note: Movement from near to far, or change from now into the future. 「寒くなっていく」= it will keep getting colder. 「持っていく」= take (along).

c:cf-49.tip: 「てくる」= coming toward me / change up to now; 「ていく」= moving away from me / change from now on. Timeline: past → present = てくる, present → future = ていく.
eg: My Japanese has gotten better. (change up to now)
It will probably get even harder from here on. (future change)

words.m: finish doing / end up doing ~ by mistake
words.note: Completion or regret. 「食べてしまった」= finished eating / ate it by accident. Colloquial form: 「～ちゃう」.
Do something to see how it is. 「食べてみる」= try eating it.
Wanting the other person to do something. 「来てほしい」= I want you to come. Note: the subject of the action is the other person.

c:cf-50.tip: 「てしまう」= completion/regret, 「てみる」= trying, 「てほしい」= wanting someone else to do something. All three are important auxiliary verbs.
eg: I lost my wallet. (regret)
Please try doing it once. (trying)
I wish you had told me sooner. (expectation of another person)

words.note: Expresses gaining an ability or habit. 「泳げるようになった」= I became able to swim.
An ability you once had disappears, or a habit stops. 「食べられなくなった」= I can no longer eat it.

c:cf-51.tip: 「ようになる」= gain a new ability / start a new habit; 「なくなる」= lose an ability / stop a habit. They form an opposing pair.
eg: I've become able to speak Japanese. (gaining an ability)
Lately I've stopped eating sweets. (stopping a habit)

words.note: Seen from someone's standpoint. 「私にとって大切な人」= someone important to me.
The target of an action, or a contrast. 「彼に対して失礼だ」= rude to him. It can also express contrast: 「～に対して～は」.
The topic or content. 「日本の文化について調べた」= researched Japanese culture.

c:cf-52.tip: 「にとって」= judgment from a standpoint, 「に対して」= target of an action / contrast, 「について」= topic. The three functions are completely different.
eg: This is difficult for students. (standpoint)
Use polite language toward seniors. (target)
We discussed environmental issues. (topic)

words.note: Not allowed because of social norms or moral duty. 「約束を破るわけにはいかない」= I can't break a promise.
Forced by circumstances to do something. 「参加せざるを得ない」= have no choice but to participate. Written style.
Double negative = must do. It stresses unavoidability more strongly than 「なければならない」.

c:cf-53.tip: 「わけにはいかない」= can't do it for moral/social reasons; 「ざるを得ない」= have no choice but to do it; 「ないわけにはいかない」= can't avoid doing it (double negative).
eg: I can't give up here. (moral/social)
It's the president's order, so I have no choice but to obey. (forced)
If I'm invited, I can't not go. (double negative = must go)

words.note: The written-style version of 「について」, more formal. 「この件に関して報告します」. Can become 「に関する＋noun」.
Using something as a basis or foundation. 「データに基づいて判断する」= judge based on data.
Adjusting as conditions change. 「能力に応じて給料が決まる」= pay is set according to ability.

c:cf-54.tip: 「に関して」= regarding (topic), 「に基づいて」= based on (foundation), 「に応じて」= adjusting to (corresponding to changes).
eg: State an opinion on this issue. (topic)
Handle it in accordance with the law. (basis)
Change measures depending on the situation. (corresponding change)

words.note: Emphasizes an extreme example. 「子供さえ知っている」= even children know. 「～さえ～ば」= if only ~.
Same meaning as 「さえ」 but more formal and written. 「名前すら知らない」= don't even know the name.
An unexpected extreme. 「先生まで笑った」= even the teacher laughed. Also common in speech.

c:cf-55.tip: 「さえ」is general, 「すら」is written, 「まで」is more colloquial and carries surprise. 「さえ～ば」(if only ~) is a fixed pattern.
eg: If you can just read kanji, you can pass. (さえ～ば)
I can't even greet people. (written style)
Even my best friend betrayed me. (surprise)

words.note: Contrast with a tone of blame or dissatisfaction. 「知っているくせに教えない」. Used only for people.
Contrast with a tone of regret or disappointment. 「せっかく来たのに留守だった」. Milder than 「くせに」.
Written style. An objective statement of contrast. 「注意したにもかかわらず、改善しなかった」. The most formal.

c:cf-56.tip: Blame → 「くせに」, regret → 「のに」, objective description → 「にもかかわらず」. 「くせに」can only be used for people.
eg: You don't do anything yourself, yet you complain. (blame)
I worked hard, but I failed. (regret)
Despite the warning, it was ignored. (objective)

words.m: on the one hand ~, on the other ~
words.note: Sets two contrasting sides side by side. 「便利な一方で、危険もある」= convenient, but also dangerous. Can also mean continuing change: 「～一方だ」.

words.m: on the other hand (the flip side)
words.note: Two opposite sides of the same thing. 「優しい反面、厳しい所もある」= gentle, but also strict in places.
A substitute or an exchange condition. 「手伝うかわりに、ご飯をおごって」= I'll help, so treat me to a meal.

c:cf-57.tip: 「一方で」sets two sides side by side, 「反面」gives the two sides of the same thing, 「かわりに」expresses a substitute or exchange condition.
eg: While the economy grows, the environment is getting worse.
The flip side of his seriousness is that he's inflexible.
Let's go on a trip instead of buying a car.

words.note: Act quickly while a state still lasts. 「暖かいうちに食べて」= eat it while it's warm. Can also mean gradually, without noticing: 「～ているうちに」.
Something happens within a period of time. 「留守の間に届いた」= it was delivered while I was out.
Mostly used as 「～ない間に」 or 「知らない間に」. Expresses something happening without anyone noticing.

c:cf-58.tip: 「うちに」= while you still can / without noticing, 「あいだに」= something happens during a period, 「まに」= while someone isn't paying attention. The 「うちに」sense of "while ~" carries urgency.
eg: You should try many experiences while you're young. (while you can)
It snowed while I was sleeping.
Time had passed before I knew it.

words.note: Strongly hypothetical. 「もし宝くじが当たったとしたら」= if I won the lottery.
A logical-inference tone. 「この説が正しいとすれば」= if this theory is correct. Leans written.

words.m: if that's so ~, in that case ~
words.note: Draws a conclusion from a premise. 「彼が犯人だとすると、辻褄が合う」= if he's the culprit, it all adds up.

c:cf-59.tip: The differences are subtle: 「としたら」= hypothetical, 「とすれば」= logical inference, 「とすると」= drawing a conclusion. They are mostly interchangeable on exams.
eg: If you had 100 million yen, what would you do?
If this theory is correct, it can be explained.
If the culprit is A, then B has an alibi.

words.m: it's the nature of ~ / how ~ is
words.note: Expresses common sense, exclamation, or reminiscence. 「時間は早く過ぎるものだ」= time really flies. 「子供の頃よく遊んだものだ」= I used to play a lot as a child.
Advice or recommendation. 「健康のためには早く寝ることだ」= for your health, you should go to bed early.
A logical conclusion. 「だから失敗したわけだ」= no wonder it failed.

c:cf-60.tip: 「ものだ」= exclamation / common sense / reminiscence, 「ことだ」= advice, 「わけだ」= logical conclusion. All three are important N2 patterns.
eg: How time flies. (exclamation)
If you catch a cold, you should rest. (advice)
You didn't get enough sleep, so no wonder you're sleepy. (logic)

words.note: Since you've decided / since things are this way, give it your all. 「やるからには勝ちたい」. Fine in both speech and writing.
Almost the same as 「からには」. Slightly more written. 「約束した以上、守るべきだ」.
The most formal and written. 「引き受けた上は、最後までやる」. The least frequently used.

c:cf-61.tip: All three mean almost the same thing: "since ~, then you must ~." Colloquialness: からには > 以上 > 上は. On exams you can treat them as near-synonyms.
eg: Since I'm going to study abroad, I want to study seriously.
Since we made a promise, we have to keep it.
Now that I've decided, I won't hesitate.

words.note: The action has started but isn't finished. 「読みかけの本」= a half-read book. 「言いかけてやめた」= stopped halfway through saying it.
Finish thoroughly. 「走りきった」= ran the whole distance. Negative 「～きれない」= can't finish.
Excessive degree. 「食べすぎた」= ate too much. 「高すぎる」= too expensive.

c:cf-62.tip: 「かける」= left unfinished midway, 「きる」= thoroughly completed, 「すぎる」= excess. These three compound verbs describe three states of an action.
eg: There's a half-eaten loaf of bread.
I ran the whole marathon.
I drank too much yesterday.

words.note: A negative tendency. 「遅刻しがちだ」= tends to be late. 「病気がちだ」= often sick.
A mild sign of something undesirable. 「風邪ぎみだ」= feel like I'm coming down with a cold. 「太りぎみ」= slightly overweight.
The kanji form of 「ぎみ」. Same usage.

c:cf-63.tip: 「がち」is about frequency (often ~), 「ぎみ」is about mild degree (a slight sign of ~). Both are negative, but 「がち」is more serious.
eg: Lately I tend to forget things. (frequent)
I'm feeling a bit tired. (mild)

words.note: Naturally suited. 「子供向きの映画」= a movie suitable for children. Stresses that the thing itself is suitable.
Made deliberately for a specific audience. 「子供向けの教材」= materials designed for children. Stresses the target audience.

c:cf-64.tip: 「向き」= naturally suited (happens to fit), 「向け」= made specially for ~ (deliberately produced).
eg: This hotel is good for families. (suitable by nature)
Japanese textbooks designed for foreigners. (deliberately designed)

words.note: 「Vた上で」= after doing ~. 「仕事の上で」= in terms of work. Both meanings are tested.
Addition. 「安い上においしい」= not only cheap but also delicious. Works for both positive and negative things.
Written style. Same as 「以上は」 and 「からには」. 「決めた上は、やるしかない」.

c:cf-65.tip: 「上で」= do after / in terms of, 「上に」= and moreover (addition), 「上は」= since (resolve). Different particles give completely different meanings.
eg: I'll reply after thinking it over carefully. (after doing)
He's smart and has a good personality too. (addition)
Now that I've accepted, I'll take responsibility. (resolve)

words.note: No matter what the condition. 「年齢を問わず」= regardless of age. Often used in recruitment and rules.
Unaffected by some factor. 「天候にかかわらず実施する」= held regardless of the weather. Stronger than 「を問わず」.
A means, or an entire period. 「インターネットを通じて」= via the internet. 「一年を通じて」= throughout the year.

c:cf-66.tip: 「を問わず」and 「にかかわらず」both mean "regardless," but the latter is stronger. 「を通じて」means a means or a whole period, so its function is different.
eg: Anyone can apply regardless of gender.
Regardless of the result, effort is what matters.
I made friends through this activity.

words.note: A highly confident inference based on evidence. 「犯人は彼に違いない」. Fine in speech and writing.
Colloquial. Carries a "it goes without saying" tone. More subjective. 「そんなの嘘に決まっている」.
The most formal written version of 「に違いない」. Used in papers and official documents.

c:cf-67.tip: Confident inference → 「に違いない」, colloquial assertion → 「に決まっている」, most formal written → 「に相違ない」.
eg: He must be the culprit.
Of course that's impossible.
His testimony is undoubtedly true.

words.note: Strongly denies the preceding statement and offers a more extreme fact. 「楽どころか、大変だった」= far from easy, it was exhausting.
Addition, going a step further. 「日本語ばかりか英語も話せる」= can speak not only Japanese but also English.
The formal written version of 「ばかりか」. 「国内のみならず海外でも」= not only domestically but also overseas.

c:cf-68.tip: 「どころか」strongly negates and reverses; 「ばかりか/のみならず」add and escalate. 「どころか」carries a "it's not just that" tone.
eg: Far from resting, I'm busier than before.
He can speak not only English but also Chinese.
It's popular not only in Japan but also overseas.

words.note: Two meanings: ① 「結果次第」= depends on the result. ② 「届き次第」= as soon as it arrives.
Multiple meanings: ① means 「メールによって」 ② cause 「地震によって」 ③ agent of a passive 「彼によって」 ④ varying depending on ~.
Using some material as a basis to create something. 「実話をもとに映画を作った」= made a movie based on a true story.

c:cf-69.tip: 「次第」= depending on the situation / as soon as, 「によって」is all-purpose (cause, means, passive), 「をもとに」= based on source material.
eg: I'll leave depending on the weather. (depends on)
I'll contact you as soon as it arrives. (as soon as)
The response differs depending on experience.
This novel was written based on a true story.

words.note: The written-style "when." For formal situations. 「お帰りの際にお立ち寄りください」= please stop by on your way back.

words.m: on the occasion of ~, at the time of ~
words.note: Facing an important moment. 「卒業に当たって一言」= a few words on the occasion of graduation. Carries a sense of solemnity.

words.m: on the occasion of ~, at the time of ~
words.note: A more formal version of 「に当たって」. Written style. 「開会にあたり」= at the opening of the meeting.

c:cf-70.tip: 「際に」is a general written "when," while 「に当たって/にあたり」stress an important occasion and are more formal.
eg: Please lock the door when you go out. (written "when")
I'd like to extend my greetings on the occasion of the new year. (formal)

words.note: Cause and effect. The first sentence is the reason, the second the result. 「雨が降った。それで中止になった。」
Taking action in response to a situation. The first sentence is the situation, the second is the action taken. 「道に迷った。そこで地図を見た。」
Something unexpected happens right after the first sentence. 「ドアを開けた。すると猫が飛び出した。」

c:cf-71.tip: 「それで」= cause-and-effect link, 「そこで」= situation → action, 「すると」= an unexpected event right after. The logical relationship differs in each.
eg: The train stopped, so I was late. (cause and effect)
I didn't understand, so I asked the teacher. (responsive action)
I opened the door, and a cat ran in. (unexpected immediate event)

words.note: The most general contrast. Fine in speech and writing. 「努力した。しかし失敗した。」
The result is unexpected. Carries surprise. 「簡単だと思った。ところが難しかった。」
The contradiction is frustrating or regrettable. 「注意した。それなのに直さなかった。」

c:cf-72.tip: 「しかし」= neutral contrast, 「ところが」= unexpected outcome, 「それなのに」= dissatisfaction/regret.
eg: I'm tired. But I'll do my best. (general contrast)
I thought it would be sunny, but it poured. (unexpected)
I taught him many times. And yet he doesn't remember. (dissatisfaction)

words.note: Moving upward or increasing. 「手を上げる」＝raise one's hand. 「レベルを上げる」＝raise the level.
Citing examples or achieving results. 「例を挙げる」＝give an example. 「成果を挙げる」＝achieve results.
Written in hiragana. As an auxiliary verb, 「V てあげる」＝do ~ for someone else. 「プレゼントをあげる」＝give a present.

c:cf-25.tip: Physically upward or increasing→「上げる」, citing examples→「挙げる」, giving or doing a favor→「あげる」.
eg: Please turn up the volume. (upward)
I explain by giving a concrete example. (citing)
I gave my friend a present. (giving)

words.note: Fixing something broken or correcting a mistake. 「車を直す」＝repair a car. 「間違いを直す」＝correct a mistake. Also used as 「V直す」＝do V again.
Treating an illness. 「病気を治す」＝cure an illness. 「風邪を治す」＝get over a cold.

c:cf-26.tip: Machines/mistakes→「直す」, illness/injury→「治す」. The compound verb 「V直す」 (redo) only uses 「直す」.
eg: I had someone fix my computer. (repair)
I rewrote my essay. (compound verb)
I got over my cold with medicine. (cure)

words.note: The most common one. Becoming accustomed to an environment or action. 「仕事に慣れる」＝get used to one's job.

words.m: to become tame; to become friendly
words.note: An animal becoming attached to people. 「犬が馴れる」＝a dog becomes tame and friendly.

words.m: to be overly familiar; to take liberties
words.note: Becoming rude through excessive familiarity. Has a negative nuance. Written language.

c:cf-27.tip: Everyday getting used to→「慣れる」, animals→「馴れる」, overly familiar→「狎れる」. The exam focuses mainly on「慣れる」.
eg: I got used to life in Japan.
The stray cat has become friendly.
Don't be overly familiar with your boss.

words.note: The broad sense of "receive". 「試験を受ける」＝take an exam. 「影響を受ける」＝be influenced.
Actually getting something in hand. 「荷物を受け取る」＝pick up a package. Can also mean "to interpret as".
Accepting mentally or institutionally. 「提案を受け入れる」＝accept a proposal.

c:cf-28.tip: 「受ける」is the broadest, 「受け取る」＝physically getting something, 「受け入れる」＝accepting mentally or institutionally.
eg: I had an interview.
Please pick up the documents.
I accepted his opinion.

words.note: One's inner feelings or sense. 「嬉しい気持ち」＝a happy feeling. Can also describe physical sensation (気持ちがいい＝feels good).
A temporary mood or physical condition. 「気分が悪い」can mean being in a bad mood or feeling unwell. Leans toward short-term states.
Mood as outwardly shown. 「機嫌がいい」＝in a good mood (visibly). Often used to describe other people.

c:cf-29.tip: 「気持ち」＝deep inner feelings, 「気分」＝a temporary state (including physical), 「機嫌」＝visible good or bad mood.
eg: I conveyed my feelings for her. (inner feeling)
I feel good today. (temporary state)
The baby is in a bad mood. (outward mood)

words.note: A claim or view on something. Implies taking a stance. 「意見を述べる」＝state an opinion.
Feelings after experiencing something. 「読書感想文」＝book report. Subjective, with no claim being made.
The result of thinking. 「考えを変える」＝change one's mind. More personal than 「意見」.

c:cf-30.tip: 「意見」＝a stance-taking opinion, 「感想」＝impressions after an experience, 「考え」＝a personal thought.
eg: Please tell me your opinion on this issue. (opinion)
I wrote my impressions of the movie. (impression)
I can't agree with his way of thinking. (personal thought)

words.note: The reason or motive for doing something. 「遅刻の理由」＝the reason for being late. Subjective; can be an excuse.
The root cause that leads to a result. 「事故の原因」＝the cause of the accident. Objective, suited to scientific analysis.
Colloquial. The background or logic of a situation. 「そういうわけで」＝for that reason. Has many grammar uses (わけがない, etc.).

c:cf-31.tip: 「理由」＝motive (why one did it), 「原因」＝root cause (why it happened), 「わけ」＝colloquial reason/circumstances.
eg: Please tell me the reason for your absence. (motive)
The cause of the fire is under investigation. (root cause)
I was busy. That's why I couldn't contact you. (circumstances)

words.note: An arranged schedule. 「明日の予定」＝tomorrow's schedule. Has a clear point in time.
A systematic plan. 「旅行の計画を立てる」＝make a travel plan. More detailed than 「予定」.
Booking a seat or service in advance. 「レストランを予約する」＝book a restaurant. Limited to reserving services.

c:cf-32.tip: 「予定」＝schedule, 「計画」＝detailed plan, 「予約」＝booking a service or seat.
eg: I'll check next week's schedule.
Let's make plans for summer vacation.
I booked a hotel.

words.note: A daily behavior cultivated on purpose. 「早起きの習慣」＝the habit of getting up early. Neutral to positive.
An unconscious small gesture or tendency. 「髪を触る癖」＝a habit of touching one's hair. Often negative.
Grammar usage. Expresses reproach. 「知っているくせに教えてくれない」＝even though you know, you won't tell me.

c:cf-33.tip: 「習慣」＝good or neutral habit (deliberate), 「癖」＝bad quirk (unconscious). 「くせに」is a grammatical connection expressing reproach.
eg: I want to get into the habit of exercising. (deliberate, positive)
I have a habit of biting my nails. (unconscious, negative)
You're strict with others even though you can't do it yourself. (reproach)

words.note: A hypothetical situation or condition. 「雨の場合」＝in case of rain. Often used to sort conditions.
A specific scene or moment. 「感動的な場面」＝a moving scene.
A position in physical space. 「集合場所」＝meeting place.

c:cf-34.tip: 「場合」＝abstract case or condition, 「場面」＝specific scene, 「場所」＝physical location.
eg: What do we do in the event of an earthquake?
My favorite scene in the movie.
Let's decide on a place to meet.

words.note: Subjectively feeling fear. Common in speech. 「お化けが怖い」＝afraid of ghosts. Expresses personal fear.
Objectively frightening things. Written language, stronger. 「恐ろしい事件」＝a horrifying incident. Can also mean "astonishing".

c:cf-35.tip: 「怖い」＝I feel afraid (subjective, spoken), 「恐ろしい」＝objectively terrifying (written, stronger).
eg: Dark roads are scary. (subjective fear)
It spread at a frightening speed. (objective, written)

words.note: Sadness from loss or misfortune. 「祖母が亡くなって悲しい」＝I'm sad because my grandmother passed away.
Feeling empty due to being alone or missing someone or something. 「一人は寂しい」＝being alone is lonely.
Suffering that is hard to bear in body or mind. 「仕事が辛い」＝work is hard/painful. Stronger than 悲しい.

c:cf-36.tip: 「悲しい」＝sad over misfortune, 「寂しい」＝empty from loneliness, 「辛い」＝unbearable suffering.
eg: The parting is sad.
I'm lonely without friends.
Overtime every day is painful.

words.note: The most common, colloquial one. Can also mean "annoying" or "nagging". 「うるさい人」＝an annoying/nagging person.
Describes a noisy, chaotic environment. Objective description. 「教室が騒がしい」＝the classroom is noisy.
Very loud, with a sense of displeasure. Can also mean "demanding". 「味にやかましい」＝particular about taste.

c:cf-37.tip: 「うるさい」is the all-purpose colloquial one, 「騒がしい」objectively describes commotion, 「やかましい」carries strong displeasure or means strict/picky.
eg: The room next door is noisy. (colloquial)
The town is in an uproar. Did something happen? (objective)
That teacher is strict about manners. (picky)

words.note: Takes effort or time, and you don't feel like doing it. 「面倒な手続き」＝a troublesome procedure. Colloquial: 「面倒くさい」.
A complicated problem that's hard to handle. 「厄介な問題」＝a thorny problem. Harder to deal with than 「面倒」.
Feeling mentally irritated. 「人間関係が煩わしい」＝human relationships are bothersome. Written language.

c:cf-38.tip: 「面倒」＝don't want to do it (laziness), 「厄介」＝hard to deal with (thorny), 「煩わしい」＝mentally irritating (mental burden).
eg: Filling out documents is a hassle. (don't want to)
A difficult patient has come in. (hard to handle)
The petty rules are annoying. (mentally)

words.note: Few in number or not often seen. 「珍しい動物」＝a rare animal. Positive or neutral.
A sense of mystery that can't be explained by common sense. 「不思議な体験」＝a mysterious experience. Carries curiosity.
A sense of strangeness that deviates from normal. 「奇妙な音」＝a strange sound. Can carry a subtly negative feel.

c:cf-39.tip: 「珍しい」＝seldom seen (rare), 「不思議」＝mysterious (inexplicable), 「奇妙」＝odd (something subtly off).
eg: This kind of flower is rare.
Something mysterious happened.
I was seized by a strange feeling.

words.note: Follows the dictionary form of a volitional verb, or noun + の. The subject stays the same (you do it for yourself). 「合格するために勉強する」.

words.m: so that ~; in order to be able to ~
words.note: Follows a non-volitional verb or potential form. Expresses hoping to reach a certain state. 「聞こえるように大きい声で話す」.

c:cf-40.tip: Volitional verb→「ために」, non-volitional verb/potential form→「ように」. Also use 「ように」when the subjects differ. This is must-know grammar for N3–N2.
eg: I study in order to get into university. (volitional verb)
I made a note so that I wouldn't forget. (non-volitional verb)
I cut it small so the child could eat it. (different subject)

words.note: Written language. A guess based on your own impression or observation. 「雨が降るようだ」. Can also be used for comparisons.
The colloquial version of「ようだ」. Nearly the same usage but more casual. 「雨みたいだ」.
A guess based on hearsay or indirect evidence. 「彼は来ないらしい」＝apparently he isn't coming. Can also mean "typical of ~".
Colloquial. Indicates a tendency. 「子供っぽい」＝childish. 「忘れっぽい」＝forgetful. Often negative.

c:cf-41.tip: Your own judgment→「ようだ (written)/みたいだ (colloquial)」, hearsay-based guess→「らしい」, tendency or trait→「っぽい」.
eg: I seem to have a fever. (own judgment, written)
He seems to be angry, you know. (colloquial)
Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow. (hearsay)
She gets angry easily. (tendency, slightly negative)

words.note: A one-time decision. 「来月から走ることにした」＝I decided to start running next month. Emphasizes the moment of decision.

words.m: try to ~; make a point of ~
words.note: Making an effort to build a habit or keep paying attention. 「毎日走るようにしている」＝I try to run every day. Emphasizes ongoing effort.

c:cf-42.tip: 「ことにする」＝making a decision (one-time), 「ようにする」＝ongoing effort (habitual). The difference between the two is often tested.
eg: I decided to study abroad next year. (one-time decision)
I try to eat vegetables. (ongoing effort)

words.note: An expectation based on reason or evidence. 「届いたはずだ」＝it should have arrived. Negative: 「はずがない」＝impossible.
A logical conclusion based on a prior cause. 「だから遅れたわけだ」＝no wonder he was late. Negative: 「わけがない」＝impossible.
What one ought to do morally or by common sense. 「謝るべきだ」＝you should apologize. Carries a tone of advice. Negative: 「べきではない」.

c:cf-43.tip: 「はず」＝should, by expectation; 「わけ」＝naturally so, by logic; 「べき」＝should, by moral duty. The "should" of each is completely different.
eg: The email should have arrived. (expectation)
If you've lived there for 3 years, of course you know it well. (naturally so)
Students should study. (moral duty)

words.note: States an objective cause. Soft, indirect tone. Preferred in formal situations and requests. Follows the plain form (na-adjective + な / noun + な).
Gives a subjective reason. More direct. Can follow polite forms. Common in speech. Can also express a volitional reason.

c:cf-44.tip: 「ので」is objective and soft, suited to formal situations; 「から」is subjective and direct, suited to speech. When asking permission, 「ので」is more polite.
eg: I have a fever, so please let me rest. (soft, formal)
I'm hungry, so let's eat something. (colloquial, direct)

words.note: The most versatile. The second event happens after the first is completed. Used for hypotheticals, certainties, and past discoveries. 「帰ったら電話して」.
A pure hypothetical condition. The result clause can't be volition, command, or request (with exceptions). 「安ければ買う」. Many fixed expressions.
The first event inevitably produces the second. Natural laws, habits. The result can't be a volitional act. 「春になると桜が咲く」.
Gives advice on a topic the other person raised. 「日本に行くなら、京都がいい」＝if you're going to Japan, Kyoto is good.

c:cf-45.tip: All-purpose→「たら」, pure hypothetical→「ば」, inevitable/habitual→「と」, the other person's topic→「なら」. That 「と」can't be followed by volition is a key exam point.
eg: As soon as I got home, I went to sleep. (after completion)
If the weather is good, let's go out. (hypothetical condition)
When you press the button, the door opens. (inevitable)
If you're going on a trip, I recommend Okinawa. (topic)

words.m: is ~ing; is in a state of having ~
words.note: In progress, or a resulting state that continues. 「窓が開いている」＝the window is open (state). 「食べている」＝is eating.
The resulting state of a transitive verb. Implies someone did it deliberately. 「窓が開けてある」＝the window has been opened (and remains so).
Doing preparation beforehand for a later purpose. 「窓を開けておく」＝open the window in advance. Contracted to 「～とく」 in speech.

c:cf-46.tip: 「ている」describes a state, 「てある」means someone did it and it remains so, 「ておく」means preparing in advance for the future. The transitive/intransitive verbs they pair with also differ.
eg: The light is on. (state)
A note has been written. (someone wrote it)
I prepared the materials for tomorrow's meeting in advance.

words.note: The most general limiter. Works with affirmative or negative. 「これだけでいい」＝this is all I need.
Must be paired with a negative. Implies "not enough" or regret. 「千円しかない」＝I only have 1,000 yen (not enough).
Stresses repetition or excess. Carries dissatisfaction. 「遊んでばかりいる」＝does nothing but play. Can also mean "just did ~" (たばかり).
Written language. Same meaning as 「だけ」but more formal. 「会員のみ」＝members only.

c:cf-47.tip: Neutral limit→「だけ/のみ (written)」, insufficient/regret→「しか＋negative」, repetition/excess→「ばかり」. "「しか」always takes a negative" is an iron rule.
eg: Only one person came. (neutral)
Only one person came. (not enough, regret)
He does nothing but complain. (dissatisfaction)
Entry is limited to authorized personnel. (written)

words.note: Past experience (た-form + ことがある) or occasional occurrence (dictionary form + ことがある).

words.m: it has been decided that ~ (not by oneself)
words.note: An external decision or the result of how things developed. 「転勤することになった」＝(the company decided) I'm being transferred.
A decision you make yourself. 「引っ越すことにした」＝(I) decided to move.

c:cf-48.tip: 「ことがある」＝experience/occasional, 「ことになる」＝decided (externally), 「ことにする」＝decided by oneself. 「になる」vs「にする」is often tested on N2.
eg: I have climbed Mt. Fuji. (experience)
I'm being transferred to Osaka from next month. (external decision)
I decided to go on a diet. (own decision)

words.note: Colloquial. Stresses a long wait, with a positive, relieved tone.
More formal or written. Stresses a long, difficult process; the tone is calmer.
Works for good or bad outcomes. Stresses that the final result is settled.
Colloquial. Often carries regret or resignation; leans more negative.

c:cf-1.tip: Positive and colloquial → 「やっと」; written → 「ようやく」; neutral outcome → 「ついに」; negative or regretful → 「とうとう」. Tests often ask about the positive vs. negative nuance of 「とうとう」 and 「ついに」.
eg: I finally passed! (colloquial, relieved)
We finally reached a conclusion. (written, long process)
They finally won the championship. (neutral, stresses the result)
In the end, he didn't come after all. (regret, resignation)

words.note: About 60–70% certain. Common in speech; a mild tone. Often paired with 「～だろう/～と思う」.
About 70–80% certain. Written style, with an undertone of worry. Often paired with 「～だろう/～と思われる」.
About 90% certain. A subjective conjecture that carries expectation or conviction. Often paired with 「～だろう/～はずだ」.
100% certain. An objective assertion or promise. Can be used for commands and rules. Often paired with 「～する/～てください」.

c:cf-2.tip: Order of certainty: たぶん < おそらく < きっと < 必ず. 「きっと」 is subjective belief; 「必ず」 is an objective guarantee.
eg: It will probably rain tomorrow. (not very sure)
I'm afraid we won't make it in time. (written, worried)
I'm sure you'll succeed. (subjective expectation)
Please be sure to submit it. (objective requirement)

words.note: An action or state is not yet finished or is still continuing. Can be affirmative (まだ食べている = still eating) or negative (まだ食べていない = haven't eaten yet).
Colloquial. Shows an action is done or a state has changed. Can also mean "no longer" (with a negative).
Written style. Stresses that the fact is settled; more formal and objective.

c:cf-3.tip: 「もう」 is colloquial and 「すでに」 is written. Both mean "already" but differ in register. 「まだ」 is their opposite. For tests, watch the 「もう＋negative = not any more」 usage.
eg: It hasn't finished yet.
They've already gone home, you know. (colloquial)
That matter has already been dealt with. (written)

words.note: Expresses strong desire or invitation. Used for requests, invitations and intentions. 「ぜひ来てください」 = Please be sure to come.
Subjective conjecture. Expresses the speaker's belief or expectation. 「きっと来る」 = (I believe) he will surely come.
Objective certainty or regularity. Can be used for promises and commands. 「必ず来る」 = he will definitely come / please be sure to come.

c:cf-4.tip: 「ぜひ」 = hope or invitation (subjective wish), 「きっと」 = conjecture or belief (subjective judgment), 「必ず」 = guarantee or rule (objective fact).
eg: Please do come visit us. (invitation)
I'm sure he'll come. (my belief)
Be sure to attend tomorrow. (rule)

words.note: Affirmative: surprisingly good. Negative: can't ~ no matter what. The two meanings differ a lot, so pay attention to context.
A high degree, close to an objective statement. Can modify positive or negative adjectives.
A degree beyond expectation, with a sense of surprise ("I didn't expect it to be so ~"). Can also mean "that's enough / no thanks."
Stresses a change or difference in degree. Often used in comparisons or when describing change.
A degree far beyond expectation, with surprise or exclamation. Stronger than 「だいぶ」.

c:cf-5.tip: Objectively high degree → 「かなり」; beyond expectation → 「けっこう」「ずいぶん」; big change → 「だいぶ」. The opposite meanings of 「なかなか」 in affirmative vs. negative sentences are a must-know test point.
eg: This movie is surprisingly interesting.
It just won't end.
It's a fairly difficult problem.
It's surprisingly delicious, isn't it?
I've gotten a lot better. (stresses change)
I was kept waiting a long time. (exclamation)

words.note: The most common. Fine in writing or speech. Objectively describes an event that happens with no warning.
Leans colloquial. Besides the meaning of 「突然」, it can show a rapid change of state (急に寒くなった).

words.m: out of the blue, right away
words.note: Colloquial. Stresses the abruptness of "skipping preparation or warning signs and just doing it." Carries a negative judgment.

c:cf-6.tip: 「突然」 is the most neutral and general; 「急に」 leans colloquial and can describe a change that speeds up; 「いきなり」 stresses abruptness, rudeness or skipped steps.
eg: An earthquake suddenly occurred. (objective description)
It suddenly started raining. (colloquial)
I was punched out of the blue. (abrupt)

words.m: going out of one's way, specially
words.note: Stresses extra effort or making a special trip for something. Often used when thanking someone or being polite.

words.m: after going to the trouble, rare chance
words.note: Stresses a rare opportunity or effort already made. Often followed by regret (～のに) or a suggestion (～だから).
Stresses that the act is intentional, not accidental. Often has a negative tone (deliberately causing trouble).

c:cf-7.tip: 「わざわざ」 = making a special trip (gratitude), 「せっかく」 = after all that effort (cherishing / regret), 「わざと」 = on purpose (blame). The three have completely different nuances.
eg: Thank you for coming all this way.
I went to the trouble of making it, but he didn't eat it.
He ignored them on purpose.

words.note: Adverb. Stresses that a change of state is fully complete. 「すっかり忘れた」 = forgot completely. Not used for listing.
Written style. Can be a noun or an adverb. Refers to the whole of what is covered.
Colloquial. Can be a noun or an adverb. Same meaning as 「すべて」 but more conversational.
The kanji spelling of 「すべて」. Used the same way.

c:cf-8.tip: 「すっかり」 modifies a change of state (completely changed), while 「すべて/全部」 means "all" in quantity. Tests often check that 「すっかり」 can't replace 「全部」.
eg: With autumn here, it has become completely cool. (change of state)
All the preparations are in place. (written)
I've finished all my homework. (colloquial)

words.note: Close to 100%. Used for quantity or degree. 「ほとんどの人」 = almost everyone. Negative: 「ほとんど～ない」 = hardly ever.
Frequency adverb. Shows a habitual action happens often. 「たいてい朝ごはんを食べる」 = usually eats breakfast.
Indicates an approximate amount or general situation. 「だいたい分かった」 = understood roughly. Can also mean "about" (だいたい3時間).

c:cf-9.tip: 「ほとんど」 = almost all (quantity), 「たいてい」 = usually (frequency/habit), 「だいたい」 = roughly (general outline).
eg: Almost all the students attended.
I'm usually at home on Sundays.
I understood the general content.

words.note: Written style. Must be used with a negative form. Firm and solemn. 「決して忘れない」 = will never forget.
Common in speech. Can go with affirmative or negative. The strongest tone. 「絶対に行く」 = will absolutely go.
Traditionally used with a negative. In casual speech it's also used affirmatively (全然大丈夫 = totally fine), but tests follow the negative pairing.
Written style. With a negative = not at all. Used alone it can be an exclamation of exasperation ("Honestly!").

c:cf-10.tip: 「決して」 = firm denial (written, must be followed by a negative); 「全然/全く」 = complete negation in degree. 「絶対」 can go with affirmative or negative. For tests, remember that 「決して」 must be followed by a negative.
eg: I will never give up. (written, firm)
I will never forgive them. (colloquial, strong)
I didn't understand at all.
I completely agree. (affirmative use)

words.note: The most general word for hypotheticals. Can go with various conditional forms such as 「～たら/～ば/～なら」.
Concessive hypothetical. Even if the assumption holds, the result doesn't change. Often followed by 「～ても/～としても」.

words.m: in the unlikely event, if by any chance
words.note: A hypothetical with extremely low probability. A cautious tone. Often used for bad things or risks. Followed by 「～たら/～の場合」.

c:cf-11.tip: 「もし」 is a plain hypothetical, 「たとえ」 is concessive (even if…, still…), and 「万が一」 stresses extremely low probability.
eg: If I have time, I'd like to go.
Even if I fail, I won't regret it.
I took out insurance just in case.

words.note: Things turned out as expected. Can also mean "after thinking it over, still ~." The colloquial contraction is 「やっぱり」.
Admiration that something lives up to its reputation. Carries a tone of respect and approval. 「さすがプロだ」 = as expected of a professional.

c:cf-12.tip: 「やはり」 = just as I thought (good or bad), 「さすが」 = living up to its reputation (admiration).
eg: As expected, he was the culprit. (as predicted)
As expected of a senior colleague, you work fast. (admiration)

words.note: Used in similes. Goes with 「～ようだ/～みたいだ」. Fine in speech or writing.
A written-style simile. Goes with 「～ようだ/～かのようだ」. More elegant than 「まるで」.

words.m: truly, typically, just the kind of
words.note: Stresses that appearance or impression fits a certain type perfectly. 「いかにも怪しい」 = looks exactly suspicious.

c:cf-13.tip: 「まるで/あたかも」 are similes (like ~), while 「いかにも」 stresses "exactly that kind of feel."
eg: It's just like a dream.
He acted as if he knew nothing.
That's a remark typical of him.

words.note: Fine in speech or writing. Rephrases or sums up what came before. The most common.
Written style. A rephrasing where both sides are fully equivalent. Often used in definitions and academic writing.
Simplifies and sums up something complicated. Has a "to put it bluntly" tone. Leans colloquial.

c:cf-14.tip: 「つまり」 is a general rephrasing, 「すなわち」 is a written, equivalent definition, and 「要するに」 is a colloquial summary.
eg: He's the company president's son, in other words, a second-generation heir.
A whale, namely, a kind of mammal. (definition)
In short, you don't have enough money, right?

words.note: Getting information. 「知っている」 = to know (state). The focus is whether you have the information.
To understand or to find out. The subject is usually a thing (～が分かる). The focus is on understanding or the result of finding out.
To grasp content or another person's thoughts thoroughly. Deeper than 「分かる」.

c:cf-15.tip: 「知る」 = whether you have the information, 「分かる」 = whether you get it, 「理解する」 = deep comprehension. Note that 「知る」 uses 「～ている」 for the state.
eg: Do you know his name? (having the information)
Do you know the answer to this question? (understanding)
Please try to understand how he feels. (deep comprehension)

words.note: To actively change a nature or state. 「予定を変える」 = change plans.
A change that happens naturally. 「天気が変わる」 = the weather changes.
Swapping between different kinds of things. 「ドルに換える」 = exchange into dollars.
Swapping old for new of the same kind. 「電池を替える」 = replace the batteries.

c:cf-16.tip: 「変」 = change in nature, 「換」 = exchange of different kinds, 「替」 = renewal of the same kind. Transitive/intransitive: 「変える」 is transitive, 「変わる」 is intransitive.
eg: I changed my hair color. (change in nature)
The seasons changed. (natural change)
I exchanged yen for dollars. (currency exchange)
I replaced the tires. (same-kind renewal)

words.note: The most general. Hearing a sound naturally, or hearing news. Can also mean "to ask" (same use as 「訊く」).
Actively listening with focus. 「音楽を聴く」 = listen to music. 「講演を聴く」 = listen to a lecture.
To actively ask. 「道を訊く」 = ask for directions. Used to distinguish in writing; in speech 「聞く」 is often written instead.

c:cf-17.tip: Passively hearing → 「聞く」, actively listening → 「聴く」, asking aloud → 「訊く」. In reading tests, watch how the kanji are distinguished.
eg: I heard a voice from the next room. (natural hearing)
I like listening to classical music. (focused listening)
Let's go ask the teacher. (asking)

words.m: to see, to look at, to watch
words.note: The most general. Actively looking. 「テレビを見る」.

words.m: to be visible, can be seen
words.note: Comes naturally into view, within sight. Not controllable. 「山が見える」 = a mountain is visible.
Potential or passive form. 「映画が見られる」 = can watch a movie. 「人に見られる」 = be seen by someone.
Watching with the aim of appreciating. 「映画を観る」「試合を観る」. Used to distinguish in writing.

c:cf-18.tip: 「見える」 = naturally visible (uncontrollable), 「見られる」 = able to see or being seen, 「観る」 = watching for enjoyment.
eg: I watch the news every morning.
You can see Mt. Fuji from here. (naturally in view)
They say we'll be able to see stars tonight. (potential)
I watched a movie at the cinema. (viewing for enjoyment)

words.note: To make something stop. 「車を止める」 = park the car. 「けんかを止める」 = stop a fight.
To stop doing something of one's own accord. 「タバコをやめる」 = quit smoking. Can be written 「止める」 or 「辞める」.
To resign from a post or leave an organization. 「会社を辞める」 = quit one's job.

c:cf-19.tip: 「止める (とめる)」 = make something stop, 「やめる」 = stop doing something yourself, 「辞める」 = resign or leave. Matching readings with kanji is a common test point.
eg: Please turn off the engine.
I gave up my diet. (quit)
I'm planning to quit my job next month.

words.note: To actively take something to a place. 「荷物を届ける」 = deliver a package.
Something arrives by itself. 「手紙が届く」 = the letter arrives. Can also mean "within reach."

c:cf-20.tip: 「届ける」 = I deliver it (transitive), 「届く」 = it arrives (intransitive). Transitive/intransitive pairs are a must-know test point.
eg: I delivered flowers to her. (transitive)
The package has finally arrived. (intransitive)

words.note: To actively gather. 「データを集める」 = collect data.
To come together naturally. 「人が集まる」 = people gather.

c:cf-21.tip: 「集める」 = I collect (transitive), 「集まる」 = things gather by themselves (intransitive). Mind the particles: を集める, が集まる.
eg: I'm collecting stamps. (transitive)
People are gathering in front of the station. (intransitive)

words.note: To actively pass a message to someone. 「気持ちを伝える」 = convey one's feelings.

words.m: to be conveyed, to be handed down (intransitive)
words.note: A message gets across naturally. 「気持ちが伝わる」 = one's feelings come across. Can also mean a culture being passed down.

c:cf-22.tip: 「伝える」 = I actively convey (を), 「伝わる」 = it naturally gets across (が).
eg: Please pass the message on to him. (transitive)
Your feelings came across fully. (intransitive)

words.note: To actively start something. 「勉強を始める」 = start studying. Also an auxiliary verb: 「V始める」 = start V-ing.
Something starts by itself. 「授業が始まる」 = class begins.

c:cf-23.tip: 「始める」 = I start something (を), 「始まる」 = it starts by itself (が). 「V始める」 is an important compound verb pattern.
eg: I started a new project. (transitive)
The movie started. (intransitive)
It began to rain. (compound verb)

words.note: Things match or suit each other. 「サイズが合う」 = the size fits. Also a compound verb: 「V合う」 = V each other.
To meet a person. 「友達に会う」 = meet a friend. A positive or neutral context.
To run into misfortune or disaster. 「事故に遭う」 = be in an accident. Used only in negative situations.

c:cf-24.tip: 「合う」 = match, 「会う」 = meet (neutral), 「遭う」 = encounter (negative). Pay attention to the kanji and particle pairings.
eg: These shoes fit my feet.
I met a friend for the first time in a long while.
Getting caught in a typhoon was rough.
